articles.text: Strikes all over the United States are so numerous that it is almost impossible to keep track of them. From the street car employes in New York city to the men on the Texas and Missouri Pacific roads there is a constant chain of strikes stretching clear across the United States. We think a low estimate of the present number of strikers in the country is 30,000, representing a loss to them in wages of over $50,000 per day.
articles.summary: Editorial note estimating 30,000 strikers nationwide.

articles.text: There seems no chance now of Dakota being admitted to the union this session of congress, unless the Democrats conclude to compromise on all the bills and admit the territory as a whole. This is a remote contingency however, and the most that will be done will probably be to submit the question of division and admission to the people at the November election. This will put the matter off another year at least.
articles.summary: Packard judges Dakota statehood unlikely this session of Congress.

articles.text: Three members of the Newark, N. J. colonization society were here Tuesday, having returned from an exploring trip and hunt up the river. The three are Wm. Germayne, well-known in this country as a hunter and who guided the Rufus Hatch party through the Yellowstone park, Wm. Huenemann and F. Ruhnke. The party started Tuesday evening for Sentinel Butte and Beach, near one of which places they think of starting a colony of several hundred families. They will make a thorough investigation of the country and the intending colonists will be guided by their decision. We will publish their report in a future issue.
articles.summary: Three Newark, N. J., colonization society men explored up the river and left for Sentinel Butte and Beach to scout a colony site.

articles.text: A characteristic point in western politics is clearly shown in our nominees for office. This is the fact that in selecting candidates for office, their being Democrats or Republicans had no weight whatever. The question as to which political party the candidate belonged to was not only never asked, but we believe never thought of. We doubt if there is a person in Billings county who knows or for that matter cares to which party any three candidates for county offices belong. The fact that they are good men is alone sufficient. Their party politics are not considered of sufficient importance to be even asked. These facts are a guarantee of better officials than could possibly be elected if party lines were closely drawn, and no matter whether Dakota is admitted or not, we hope that the political question will never effect the choice of Billings county's officials. On national questions where the success of a party is at stake it is well to take sides. In county affairs where one political party may greatly overbalance the other, honesty and capacity are the only things to be considered.
articles.summary: Editorial praising the nonpartisan selection of Billings county nominees.

articles.text: The Republicans of New York are so badly demoralized that they have solicited Conkling to again lead them to victory. Whether or not he assumes the leadership, the fact of his being asked, is the highest compliment that could be given him. Although he committed the greatest political blunder of the nineteenth century in resigning his seat in the Senate and not being sure of re-election, he is head and shoulders above any Republican leader in New York.
articles.summary: Editorial on New York Republicans asking Roscoe Conkling to lead them again.

articles.text: A curious trait of states' cows is that of "caching" their calves. For several days after birth, they generally keep their calves hidden in some secure place, visiting them once or twice a day and perhaps getting their own feed a mile or more away. Strange as it may seem this practice is much more common among gentle states' cattle than any other class.
articles.summary: Note on 'states' cows hiding their newborn calves.

articles.text: M. Wadsworth of the Bad Lands cattle Co., intends sowing several different kinds of grass seeds this season, and in the future, sowing the one giving the best satisfaction, in a hay meadow. Gregor Lang of the Neimmela ranch will do the same thing and we hope to see the plan generally adopted. Every range has on it somewhere, at least a few acres of ground that can be profitably sown to hay and before many years we expect to see the raising of hay considered as necessary as any other part of ranch work.
articles.summary: Wadsworth and Gregor Lang plan to test grass seeds for hay meadows.

articles.headline: A Branded Bear.
articles.text:
A Branded Bear.

A gang of Colorado cowboys the other day found a grizzly bear in a favorable location, surrounded and lassoed him and then branded him in half a dozen places with the ranch mark. Bruin was then turned loose and by the law of the stock regions, will be recognized as the property of the men whose brand he carries around with him. The leader of the cowboys who played the prank was Webb Cross, a young fellow well known in Nebraska and a graduate of the Journal establishment.—[Nebraska State Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped item: Colorado cowboys lasso and brand a grizzly bear.

articles.headline: Is Old Beef Tough?
articles.text:
Is Old Beef Tough?

I wish here to protest against the prevalent idea that old meat is tough. Never was there a greater fallacy. The age of the animal has nothing whatever to do with it and the fact is, the toughest and most tasteless meat is that of a two-year-old steer, kept fat from birth and then shipped to market where he will arrive in a shrinking condition. On the contrary, the most tender, juicy and highest flavored meat is that of an old animal, a cow or even a work steer, no matter how old, if fattened rapidly and killed when in a thriving condition. All meat is more or less tough when the animal is losing flesh and the opposite, tender and juicy if the animal is gaining rapidly, and if all your meat is killed when the animal is losing flesh, you never get any really good meat. The change can be noticed in the meat before the eye detects it in the animal's condition.—[Drover's Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped item arguing old beef is not tough if fattened rapidly; continues at top of column 7.

articles.text: The weather now gives such fair promise of staying good, that no alarm is felt for the safety of the cattle. They are thinner than usual at this season of the year, but will pick up instead of losing until new grass starts. Calves are being dropped freely and are doing well, although their mothers are generally in poor condition.
articles.summary: Good weather eases fears for range cattle; calves doing well.

articles.text: A number of our stock exchanges contain editorial comments on the International range association which must be prompted by petty jealousy or spite. They entirely ignore the fact of the universal good such an organization will be to the range industry and allow themselves to criticize the association harshly on account of small defects that may not take away the least from the good the association will do. The International association stands in exactly the same relation to local associations that these associations do to the individual cattlemen. Individually, almost nothing can be accomplished. United, no one will dare do them an injustice. The International association has "taken the bull by the horns" in the outset, and if backed up properly by the state and territoreal associations will effectually prevent the introduction of infectious diseases and see to it that the price of range cattle is not manipulated to suit the taste of three or four Chicago packers. It is utterly impossible for local associations to cope with these tasks successfully. The International range association, backed by all local associations, will be in a position to demand and command justice. We earnestly hope that no narrow-minded policy will cause associations to be luke-warm[?] in their allegiance[?] to the International association. Business principles should prove to all, that the new organization is worthy of their warmest assistance.
articles.summary: Editorial defending the International Range Association against critics in the stock press.

articles.headline: Origin of Native Cattle.
articles.text:
Origin of Native Cattle.

The origin of the so-called native cattle on this continent is credited to a small herd brought by Columbus on his second voyage. Other Spanish navigators brought small herds from time to time, while in 1553 the Portuguese landed both cattle and hogs in Nova Scotia. Cattle are said to have been introduced into Canada in 1608, and Virginia was reported to have 500 head of cattle in 1620. At that time stringent laws prohibited the killing of any domestic animals. Cattle were introduced into New England in 1624. It is said that in those days the red color depreciated the price of cattle, a red calf being more likely to be mistaken for a deer by the wolves and killed than a black one.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped item on the origin of native American cattle.

articles.text: "The loss of cattle on the ranges in western Kansas and eastern Colorado by the terrible cold weather is beyond almost any comparison heretofore made. A report received here a few days ago makes an estimate of 25,000 head as being large enough to cover the losses. In a trip from Emporia to Syracuse, sixteen miles this side of the Colorado line, your correspondent is positive that he saw dead bodies and hides enough from the car windows to almost make that amount. In one place a bunch of 100 were found together, all dead, while in the hollows passed, where the snow had been heavily drifted, hundreds of horns, heads, and parts of bodies could be seen protruding from the snow as it was being rapidly melted away from the carcasses. And this is not all, for thousands of animals may be seen tottering along, partly frozen, and so thin and gaunt that it seemed the wind could almost blow through them. Cattlemen are evidently desirous of making as light of the matter as possible, but, in the language of a citizen of western Kansas 'there will be a big stench when warm weather comes."—[Emporia, Kan. telegram.
articles.summary: Clipped report of heavy winter cattle losses in western Kansas and eastern Colorado.

articles.text: Last Thursday evening, Sheriff Sebastian came down from Dickinson and went back in the morning with Fred Banan in custody, on the charge of assault and battery. It seems that Fred had a dispute with a newsboy on the train a few evenings before and had worn him out considerably. Before Justice Starr, his fine and costs amounted to $64. Fred does not consider the sensence a just one and will serve out the fine and costs in preference to paying them.

articles.headline: Notice of Election.
articles.text:
Notice of Election.

Notice is hereby given that on the Second (2nd.) Monday in April, 1886, at the following place, viz.: at the town of

Medora,

in the County of Billings, an election will be held for the following officers of said county of Billings, in said Territory of Dakota, in the organization of said county:

Three County Commissioners,
One Register of Deeds,
One County Clerk,
One Sheriff,
One Assessor,
One Judge of Probate,
One County Treasurer,
One County Surveyor,
One Coroner,
One Superintendent of Public Schools,
Four Justices of the Peace,
Four Constables,
and also for the temporary location of the
County seat of said county,
which election will be open at the hour of eight o'clock in the morning and will continue open until five o'clock in the afternoon of the same day.

Dated this 20th. day of January, 1886.

[Seal.] Gilbert A. Pierce, Governor.

M. L. McCormack, Secretary.
articles.summary: Governor Pierce's notice of the first Billings county election at Medora, second Monday in April 1886.
